entries.title: Parametric Point Cloud Blend Space
entries.body:
PPCBS is a three-dimensional blend space for building complex locomotion systems. Beyond grounded locomotion, it covers states such as swimming and flying, and its additional input lets grounded locomotion sample data such as slope or stance.

## Highlights

- **Multiple blend algorithms.** Each use case can use the algorithm that suits it instead of a single guessed or hard-coded method, so designers can build the gameplay animation logic they need without restrictions.
- **Flexible spaces.** Omnidirectional movement spaces, provided the sampled space is lined up correctly, as well as non-planar movement behaviors.
- **Phase synchronization.** Cyclic animations are kept in phase, avoiding muddy transitions, foot sliding and bunny hopping in grounded and swimming locomotion alike.

## Runtime and Editor Showcase

<iframe width="560" height="315"
src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/YPJ0_ISq-yg"
title="YouTube video"
frameborder="0"
allowfullscreen>
</iframe>

---

PPCBS is still experimental, and its editor tools and visibility need further iteration. I plan to release an evaluation build for testing.

entries.title: Profiling Animation Graphs
entries.body:
Profiling animation graphs can be difficult, especially in large systems where evaluation or code execution depends on nodes throughout the graph and on valid node references.

In simpler cases, some graph evaluation can be overridden with **pose caching**. This works well as long as dependencies like these don't prevent the graph from evaluating correctly, but even then the process becomes tedious.

`stat anim` and Unreal Insights traces give a general overview of which systems affect performance, but they only hint at where the cost lies and leave room for guesswork.

To speed this up, I created two custom nodes that measure the cost of specific sections of an animation graph, without unplugging layers or disconnecting nodes.

![[Pasted image 20260301180014.png]]

Each node creates a **stat scope cycle counter** named after its assigned section. Placing several of them throughout the graph shows which sections are the most expensive when optimization becomes necessary:

![[Pasted image 20260301180607.png]]

`Stat PATK_Profiling 1` enables the custom stat group, confirms that the scope counters are registered, and shows the timing of each instrumented section:

![[Pasted image 20260301181028.png]]

## In Practice

![[2026-03-01 18-18-26.mp4]]

![[Pasted image 20260301182237.png]]

![[2026-03-01 18-26-36.mp4]]

With the cost of each section visible, unoptimized features can be found and addressed directly.

entries.title: Physia - Procedural Active Ragdoll Framework
entries.body:
> Work in progress. A more detailed write-up will follow.

Physia articulates **physical bodies procedurally**, using solvers to fill the gaps where authored animation struggles or would require extensive animation coverage.

<iframe width="560" height="315"
src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/vGiD6DGbWx0"
title="YouTube video"
frameborder="0"
allowfullscreen>
</iframe>

The video combines older and newer development footage.

## Implemented

- A native API for articulating humanoid bodies.
- ImGui debugging tools to track the system's state and make it easier to use.
- Analytical solvers for bracing, balancing, foot placement and more.
- A custom IK solver for arms and legs.
- A rewrite from world space to ego space, primarily in preparation for machine learning.
- Parts of the functionality exposed to Blueprint graphs.

## Next Steps

- Make the system reliable, efficient and intuitive for designers to use.
- Expose more functionality to Unreal's Blueprint graphs.
- Expose native functions and solvers to help with more complex tasks.

## Further Out

- A machine learning pipeline for training physical models.
- Pre-trained models for stepping and balancing, for more grounded and natural results out of the box.

entries.title: Concept and Introduction
entries.body:
## Limitations of Traditional Look-At Solvers

Traditional look-at solvers usually offer limited control. Most simply use a look-at constraint to orient a bone towards a point of interest in the world. This works to a degree, but people do more than that.

More complex solvers can introduce problems across poses. Their influence may blend out in some situations, which can easily break the overall pose. Solving look-at constraints additively on top of existing animation causes further issues: if the authored animation already has the character looking left, the head may overextend and overshoot the target before settling back.

## A State-Driven Approach

My approach adds a **state machine** to the look-at solve, allowing finer control across states such as gait, stance, emotion and context.

## Conveying Emotion Beyond Facial Expressions

Facial expressions are not the only way to convey emotion; posture plays a key role as well. An angry character may tilt their head down, and an intimidated one may look down. Looking up can convey dominance, while tilting the head to either side adds nuance. Subtle movements like these make a character more believable.

## Eyes

The eyes are solved as part of the same system, with their behavior parametrized, since they change how a character feels in states such as being drunk or under the influence of substances. Separating these characteristics exposes full control over how a character feels in each of the states above.

## Solving Chains

Each bone's contribution to the authored pose can be controlled individually, which makes the system easy to dial in.

To keep evaluation inexpensive, the chain is solved from root to tip. I considered iterating forward and backward passes to distribute the contribution across the whole chain, but this was not necessary: the simple approach already gives great results, especially combined with the state machine.

A tip-to-root solve would be slightly more expensive, and without a forward and backward pass it could be problematic, as the position of the chain may shift unpredictably.

## Constraints and Anatomical Correctness

As with constraints for a physically articulated body, parent-space constraints are crucial for keeping joints in natural poses and ensuring the solver never produces anatomically incorrect orientations. These constraints can also be modified at runtime.

## Blending Between Configurations

Look-at configurations switch based on a state machine, and the look-at node blends between them naturally, avoiding pops regardless of how complex the new configuration is. Designers can create situation-specific configurations and blend between them with a state machine, either natively or through Unreal's editor node graphs.

## Flexibility Across Characters

The system handles complex characters and a variety of creatures, so the same solver can be reused without a custom solution for each archetype. Even a Medusa with fifty snakes on her head works.

Rig conventions and transforms differ across rigs, so these settings are exposed explicitly rather than assumed.

## Closing Thoughts

I hope this gives a clear idea of the approach for anyone who wants to build a similar or better system. I have intentionally left out code snippets and source code: the goal is to provoke thought and let you design a solution based on your own ideas.

The results are shown in the [[Showcase]].

entries.title: Getting Started
entries.body:
If you haven't already, start by downloading the toolkit: [[Procedural Animation Toolkit]].

## Adding the Node

Open the Anim Graph and navigate to the **Procedural Anim Layer**. Right-click and search for the **PA_TK_LookAt** node to add it.

![[Screenshot 2026-03-01 153436.png]]

## Node Settings

The node looks simple at first; its settings are in the **Details** panel.

![[Pasted image 20260301154152.png]]

The **Fallback** sections can be ignored: they exist only for backwards compatibility with earlier iterations.

- **Look At Target Location** (annotated first) defines the point in **world space** the character should focus on.
- **Look At Config** (second) holds all the data needed to solve the look-at.

To expose the config:

1. Click the **Bind** button and expose the pin.
2. Drag off the node and **promote it to a variable**.
3. **Compile and save.**

## The Look At Config

![[Pasted image 20260301155506.png]]

- **Bones** holds a collection of structured bone configurations for the affected bone chain, covered below.
- **Eyes** works the same way, but is solved differently.
- **Max Look At Angle in Degrees** applies per bone, always relative to the parent. Set it to **90** for now.
- **Look At Target Smooth Speed** uses **spherical interpolation** to smooth the movement towards the target when the focus changes, relative to the component (the character).
- **Config Blend Speed** controls how quickly a newly selected config blends in. It matters when configs are switched by a **state machine** and can otherwise be ignored.

## Adding Bones

Add a bone configuration:

![[Pasted image 20260301160749.png]]

Then assign the first bone in the chain:

![[Pasted image 20260301160945.png]]

Next are the **local-space axis conventions**: the **forward axis**, which should point towards the target, and the **up axis**. Open the rig and verify which axes it uses.

![[Pasted image 20260301161514.png]]

In this rig, Y is forward and X is up:

![[Pasted image 20260301161813.png]]

**Forward Axis Offset Rotation** can be tweaked later, **at runtime**. Sometimes a bone doesn't point exactly at the target; this offset adjusts the vector so the bone aligns with where it should look.

## Constraint Limits

![[Pasted image 20260301162352.png]]

These limits define the joint's **constraint space**. Relative to the parent, they set how far the joint can move, using a **swing-twist** solve. They can be **adjusted at runtime**, which makes configuring a look-at much easier.

- **Constraint Frame Rotation** offsets the constraint space, similar to **Forward Axis Offset Rotation**. Adjust it **after** setting the forward axis offset so everything aligns correctly.
- **Max Angular Speed (Deg)** is unused and can be ignored.
- **Look At Blend Weight** controls the overall procedural contribution to the pose.
- **Blend Damping Speed** controls how quickly the bone orients towards the target.

Now add the remaining bones, **verifying the axis conventions** for each. To speed this up, duplicate a bone configuration several times and change the affected bone. Spine chains usually follow a similar convention, but always double-check against the asset.

## The Baseline

![[Pasted image 20260301164404.png]]

The setup should now look similar to this.

The **Target Location** is still at **world 0,0,0** unless you have already changed it, so move to a location close to it. Alternatively, drag a sphere into the level, copy its world location and set that value in the Anim Graph.

After spawning into the world, the character should already be looking at something, though perhaps not exactly as intended. Dock the Anim Graph editor on the opposite side of the PIE viewport so the constraints can be edited and visualized in real time.

With the struct open on one side and PIE on the other, enter this command to visualize the constraints while editing them:

```
a.proc.lookat.debug 1
```

![[Pasted image 20260301165751.png]]

Once the config is tuned, save the adjusted values and duplicate the config to use as a **baseline**, named **`LookAt_Configurator`**.

Duplicate it again for each state you need: the baseline can represent **idle/standing**, with additional configs per **gait** and **stance**. When using a **state machine**, also create one named **`Runtime_LookAt_Config`**. A setup could look like the one in [[State Machine Setup]].

## Beyond Look-Ats

The system can solve **aim offsets** as well as general look-ats. I have also tested driving an arm chain with a **flashlight**; it wasn't designed for that, but it works, as shown in the [[Showcase]].

It has also been tested for **directional blocking in combat** and for **movement during gaits**, where it expanded the range of motion without any additional animation authoring. More will follow soon.
